criteria.name: FLUENCY & COHERENCE
criteria.feedback: Part 2 da uzun javobni davom ettirding. Qayta boshlash va “I usually”, “so that’s it” takrorlari oqimni susaytirdi.

criteria.name: LEXICAL RESOURCE
criteria.feedback: Fikr yetdi, lekin “get rid of tired”, “work so bad” kabi birikmalar tabiiy emas. So‘z topolmaganda fikrni sodda qayta ayt.

criteria.name: GRAMMAR
criteria.feedback: O‘tmish va hozirgi zamonni aralashtirish, “if I will go”, “can tracking”, “going to studying” kabi xatolar ko‘p bo‘ldi.

criteria.name: PRONUNCIATION
criteria.feedback: Yozma matndan tovush, urg‘u va ohangni tekshirib bo‘lmaydi.

highlights.text: Eski tartibing, qilgan o‘zgarishing va natijani ketma-ket tushuntirding. Vaqtlarni aniq ayt: about a year ago va two months ago.

highlights.text: Har javobni fikr → sabab → aniq misol → qisqa izoh tartibida tuz. Bir savolda bitta fikrni yetarlicha rivojlantir.

questions.question: How many hours do you usually sleep at night?
questions.original: I usually sleep eight or seven hours during days, but it is mostly related when I begin or when I go to the bed for sleep. If I sleep at 12 p.m., I think I will wake up five and get up six. But I usually sleep at 10 p.m. and I wake up four or five, and this is enough for me.
questions.sample: I normally **get a solid seven hours** of sleep, although it depends on my schedule. I try to **wind down** at about ten and **stick to a routine** during the week. When I do that, I tend to **wake up feeling refreshed**. If I stay up unusually late, I may sleep a little longer the next morning to **make up for lost sleep**.

questions.question: Describe a change you made that helped you sleep better.
questions.original: Today I will say my small habits, what they changed my fully life. For example, my daily routine, my sleep time, my wake up time, and for example, what helped me change my sleep time. Around two years ago, one year ago, I usually sleep at 12 p.m. or 1 a.m. It's midnight. So, and I wake up around 7 or 6 a.m. and I felt bad, and I couldn't sleep better and enough. So I tired. I felt tired during day. But around two months ago, I sit up. I changed my sleep time, and I go to bed at around 9 p.m, and I started reading books. And I didn't use my phone before 30 minutes before bed. It helps me better and stay calm before sleep. And I sleep at 10 p.m. or 10 past 30 minutes, and I wake up. I usually wake up at 4 or 5 a.m. It helps me to do more things in the morning, and when I wake up, I immediately drink one glass of water. It helps me better and, like, maybe not tired. And why I decided it, because before this decision, my work, I made a lot of mistakes in my work, and I couldn't study effectively, and my time also so effectless, and it looked like less than others. And I started and I decided to this decision, and it helped me more, give me more time and more chance. And whatever before the sleep, I usually do cardio for reduce stress. So, that's it. And it affected effectively sleep and easily wake up.
questions.sample:
I’d like to describe a small but surprisingly effective change to my evening routine. Until a couple of months ago, I had **fallen into a bad habit** of **staying up past midnight**. I would tell myself I was only going to check one message, but I often ended up **scrolling through social media** for an hour. Because I still needed to get up early for my studies, the lack of sleep began to **take a toll on my concentration**. I felt sluggish in the morning and sometimes had to reread the same page several times.

Eventually, I **made a conscious decision** to change that pattern. I began to **set a regular bedtime**, usually around ten o’clock, and **put my phone out of reach** about half an hour beforehand. Instead of staring at a screen, I would **wind down with a book**. I chose something enjoyable rather than difficult study material, so reading actually felt like a break. At first, I was tempted to check my phone, but after a week or two it became easier to **stick with the change**.

The biggest difference is how I feel in the morning. I don’t claim that every night is perfect, but I’m much more likely to **wake up feeling refreshed** and begin studying without that heavy, distracted feeling. I also have a little quiet time to plan my day. What I like about this change is that it didn’t require a complicated system: I simply replaced one unhelpful habit with a calmer one. I hope to keep doing it even if my timetable changes when I study abroad.

cards.e: Until a couple of months ago, I had fallen into a bad habit of staying up past midnight.

questions.question: Why do you think many people get less sleep nowadays?
questions.original: In my opinion, people sleep less now than past because they work so bad, and in my opinion they try hard work or hard study, and I think they think sleep is not important, as if they are sleep, they just wasting of their time. But in my opinion it's so, like, stupid stuff, because sleep is the most important thing in our routine. Because sleep helps us to rest and relax and more effectively to do something, or more effectively to learning something. So I think they are tough, because this action, this situation.
questions.sample: I think **long working hours** are part of the explanation, but technology also plays a role. With **constant digital stimulation**, it’s easy to keep answering messages or watching videos long after we intended to go to bed. Some people also **prioritise productivity over rest**, as though an extra hour awake automatically means an extra hour of useful work. In reality, those habits can **cut into sleep time** without producing much benefit. Staying up to finish a task may occasionally be necessary, but doing it every night is often **a false economy** if you’re exhausted the following day.

questions.question: Should schools and workplaces change their schedules to help people get enough sleep? Why or why not?
questions.original: In my opinion, the first people should change their thoughts about sleep, and schools and workplaces should change their schedule to help people get enough sleep. Why? You know, many schools and workplaces set up their schedules at night, even at night. And if someone should earn money, he tries, or people try to work even at night, and it affects their mental health and health. And so they couldn't get enough sleep. But if the schools and workplaces change their schedules, they can sleep better. So that's it.
questions.sample: In some cases, yes. For example, **early start times** can be difficult for students who travel a long way, while people who **work irregular shifts** may struggle to maintain a consistent routine. Where practical, **flexible working hours** could give people more control over their mornings. Schools and employers should also look at whether workloads leave enough time to **protect sleep quality**. Of course, hospitals and other essential services cannot simply close at night, so the goal is to **find a workable balance** rather than impose one timetable on everyone.

questions.question: Do you think technology makes it easier or harder for people to maintain a healthy lifestyle?
questions.original: In my opinion, technology makes it easier for people to maintain a healthy lifestyle. Why? Because you can tracking, or you can check your health, like heart, blood pressure, and technology helps us to see how they do some work, some jobs, like it affects people's health. For example, factory or mining, or, etc. In the past, I would give one example. In the past, in our country, people worked agricultural relentlessly at even night and during the day, and their health was bad, and they usually suffered from diseases like tired and insomnia, cancer. Technology now working instead of them, and technology in our country health rate improved day by day, year by year.
questions.sample: It can do either, depending on how people use it. A watch may help someone **track health metrics** or provide **reminders to move** during a long day at a desk. On the other hand, streaming and social media can encourage **sedentary habits**, especially if they replace exercise or sleep. I wouldn’t call technology itself healthy or unhealthy. The important thing is to **use technology mindfully**: let it support your goals without letting it dominate your free time. For me, that distinction is what **tips the balance**.

cards.e: A watch may help someone track health metrics or provide reminders to move during a long day at a desk.

questions.question: Who should take more responsibility for people’s health: individuals or governments?
questions.original: The first and foremost, people take more responsibility for their health because if they set up their schedules correctly and tightly, and if they avoid some bad habits like smoking, drinking wine, they will not suffer this, like heart and blood pressure. And if they have some, like simple diseases like cough or sneeze, they should immediately go to the doctor without self, because many people know if they are cough, they immediately consume pill without asking or without discussion with doctor, and ultimately these pills cause sometimes these or more and dangerous diseases when they are self.
questions.sample: I’d say responsibility is shared. Individuals have to **take personal responsibility** for their daily routines and **make informed choices** about their habits. But governments can **create supportive environments**, for example by ensuring that neighbourhoods have places where people can be active and **reliable health information** is easy to find. People’s options also depend on their income and working hours, so telling everyone simply to “try harder” overlooks real constraints. In my view, public policy should remove unnecessary barriers, while individuals **set sensible boundaries** and make use of the opportunities available to them.

cards.e: Individuals have to take personal responsibility for their daily routines and make informed choices about their habits.

Schools should share reliable health information with students.

questions.question: What can governments do to encourage people to develop healthier habits?
questions.original: I would say governments today encourage people to develop healthier habits. For example, they should schedule setups schedules respectively, and they may force people to do exercise, cardio exercise, or just exercise in the morning. Every people should do this. They offer people some events, and they speak and say... gossip people, and they teach them to develop and evolve their healthier habits. And they should ban, like smoking, drinking wine, and in other situations, like stuff.
questions.sample: Governments could begin with **public awareness campaigns** that explain practical habits in clear language. They could also invest in **safe public spaces**, such as parks and walking routes, so that being active is convenient rather than expensive. Schools and public institutions can **lead by example** by making room for movement during the day. I think the aim should be to **make healthy choices accessible**, not force everyone into the same routine. That approach is more likely to support **long-term behaviour change** because people can adapt the advice to their own circumstances.

cards.e: Governments could begin with public awareness campaigns that explain practical habits in clear language.
